alts: what does generative mean in ai
entries.a: Generative AI is AI that creates new content such as text, images, audio or code, instead of only sorting or scoring existing data. It learns patterns from large amounts of examples and produces new output that follows those patterns. Chat assistants and image generators are common examples.

Deep learning is a kind of machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers. Each layer learns a slightly more abstract pattern than the one before. It powers most modern speech, vision and language models, but it needs a lot of data and computing power.

A neural network is a model made of many small connected units, loosely inspired by brain cells. Each connection has a weight, and training adjusts those weights so the network maps inputs to the right outputs. It is the basic building block of deep learning.

entries.q: What is a transformer in AI?
entries.a: A transformer is a neural network design that reads a whole sequence at once and uses attention to decide which parts relate to each other. It trains well on very large datasets and runs efficiently on GPUs. Almost all large language models today are built on transformers.

entries.q: What is attention in a language model?
entries.a: Attention is the step in a transformer where each token looks at the other tokens and weighs how relevant they are. It is how the model links a pronoun back to the right noun, or a question to the right part of a document. The cost of attention grows quickly with input length, which is one reason long prompts are slower.

alts: data used to train a model
entries.a: Training data is the set of examples a model learns from. Its quality, coverage and labels shape what the model can do and where it will fail. If a case type is missing from training data, the model will usually handle it poorly.

entries.q: What are training, validation and test sets?
entries.a: Data is split so a model learns on one part and is checked on parts it has never seen. The training set teaches the model, the validation set helps tune settings, and the test set gives the final honest score. Mixing them up gives scores that look better than real performance.

Overfitting is when a model learns the training examples too closely, including their noise, and then does badly on new data. You spot it when training scores are high but test scores are much lower. More data, simpler models and regularization help.

Underfitting is when a model is too simple to capture the real pattern, so it does badly even on its training data. It often means the model lacks useful inputs or capacity. The fix is better features, a more capable model or more training.

entries.q: What is classification in machine learning?
entries.a: Classification is a task where the model assigns each input to one of a set of categories. Examples are spam or not spam, or routing a complaint to the right product group. Results are judged with measures such as precision, recall and a confusion matrix.

entries.q: What is regression in machine learning?
entries.a: Regression is a task where the model predicts a number rather than a category. Examples are forecasting next month's demand or estimating how long a batch review will take. Errors are measured as how far predictions are from the real values.

Clustering groups items that look similar without being told the groups in advance. It is used to find natural segments, such as types of complaints or customer groups. A person still has to look at each cluster and decide what it means.

Supervised learning trains a model on examples that already have the right answer attached, called labels. The model learns to map inputs to those answers. Classification and regression are the two main kinds.
Unsupervised learning finds structure in data that has no labels. Clustering and anomaly detection are common examples. It is useful for exploring data before you know exactly what to predict.

Reinforcement learning trains a model by letting it take actions and giving it rewards or penalties based on the results. Over many tries it learns which actions lead to better outcomes. It is used in games, robotics and in the post-training of language models.

RLHF stands for reinforcement learning from human feedback. People compare or rate model answers, and those preferences are used to train the model toward more helpful and safer responses. It is one of the post-training steps that turns a raw language model into a useful assistant.

NLP, natural language processing, is the field of making computers work with human language. It covers tasks like classifying text, pulling out names and dates, translating and summarizing. Large language models now handle many NLP tasks that used to need separate models.

Computer vision is the field of making computers understand images and video. Common tasks are spotting defects on a production line, reading labels and counting objects. In manufacturing it is often used for automated visual inspection.

OCR, optical character recognition, turns images of text, such as scanned forms or photos of labels, into machine-readable text. It is often the first step before an AI can read paper records. Accuracy drops with poor scans, handwriting and complex tables, so results need checking.

Intelligent document processing, or IDP, combines OCR, layout understanding and AI to pull structured data out of documents like invoices, certificates and batch records. The output is usually fields in a table or JSON. A person typically reviews low-confidence or high-risk fields.

Speech to text, also called automatic speech recognition or ASR, converts spoken audio into written text. It is used for meeting transcripts, call notes and voice commands. Accuracy depends on audio quality, accents and domain vocabulary.

Text to speech, or TTS, turns written text into spoken audio. It is used in voice assistants, accessibility tools and phone systems. Modern TTS sounds natural but can still mispronounce technical terms.

Named entity recognition, NER, finds and labels things like people, companies, places, dates and product codes in text. It turns free text into structured fields. A common use is pulling lot numbers and dates out of complaint descriptions.

Sentiment analysis scores whether a piece of text is positive, negative or neutral. It is used on customer feedback, reviews and support tickets. It misreads sarcasm and domain language easily, so treat it as a rough signal.

entries.q: What is a feature in machine learning?
entries.a: A feature is one input value a model uses to make a prediction, such as temperature, batch size or supplier. Good features carry real signal about the outcome. Feature engineering is the work of building better features from raw data.

Data labeling is attaching the correct answer to each example, such as marking an image as defect or no defect. Labels are what supervised models learn from and what evaluations score against. Labels from real domain experts are worth much more than quick guesses.

A loss function is a number that measures how wrong a model's predictions are during training. Training tries to make this number as small as possible. Choosing the right loss decides what kind of mistakes the model cares about most.

Gradient descent is the method most models use to learn. It measures which way each weight should move to reduce the loss, then nudges every weight a little in that direction, over and over. Backpropagation is the technique that computes those directions efficiently in neural networks.

entries.q: What is an epoch in training?
entries.a: An epoch is one full pass of the training data through the model. Training usually runs for several epochs. Too few and the model underfits, too many and it can overfit.

A hyperparameter is a setting chosen before training, not learned from data, such as the learning rate or number of layers. Changing hyperparameters can change results a lot. Tuning means trying different values and keeping the ones that score best on validation data.

A confusion matrix is a table that counts a classifier's right and wrong answers by type: true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives. It shows which mistakes the model makes, not just how many. In quality work, missing a real defect is usually worse than a false alarm, and the matrix makes that visible.

Precision is the share of items the model flagged that were really positive. Recall is the share of real positives the model managed to find. You usually trade one against the other, so pick based on which error costs more.

The F1 score combines precision and recall into one number using their harmonic mean. It is high only when both are good. It is handy for comparing models, but always look at precision and recall separately too.

entries.q: What does accuracy mean for a model?
entries.a: Accuracy is the share of all predictions that were correct. It can mislead when one class is rare: if only a few items in a hundred are defects, a model that always says no defect still looks very accurate. Use precision, recall and per-class results alongside it.

LoRA, low-rank adaptation, is a way to fine-tune a large model by training small extra matrices instead of changing all its weights. It needs far less memory and storage than full fine-tuning. The small adapter can be swapped in and out of the same base model.

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning, or PEFT, is a family of methods that adapt a large model by training only a small number of extra or selected parameters. LoRA is the best known example. It makes fine-tuning possible on modest hardware.

Full fine-tuning updates every weight of a pre-trained model on new data. It can give the deepest change in behaviour but needs a lot of GPU memory and good data. Most teams try prompting, RAG or PEFT methods first.

Instruction tuning, a form of supervised fine-tuning, trains a model on many examples of instructions paired with good answers. It teaches a raw pre-trained model to follow requests rather than just continue text. It is a standard step in building chat assistants.

Distillation trains a smaller student model to copy the outputs of a larger teacher model. The student is cheaper and faster while keeping much of the teacher's skill on the target task. It is a common way to make a model practical for high volume use.

Quantization stores a model's weights with fewer bits, for example 8 or 4 bits instead of 16. The model then needs less memory and often runs faster, with some loss of quality. It is how large open-weight models fit on a single GPU or a laptop.

An inference server is software that loads a model and answers prediction requests over an API. It handles batching, memory and many users at once. Teams self-hosting open-weight models use one so applications can call the model like any other service.

entries.q: What is a GPU and why does AI need it?
entries.a: A GPU, graphics processing unit, is a chip that does many simple calculations in parallel. Neural networks are mostly large matrix multiplications, which GPUs run much faster than normal CPUs. GPU memory also decides how large a model you can run.

A vector database stores embeddings and finds the ones closest to a query embedding quickly. It is the usual store behind semantic search and RAG. Many normal databases now offer vector search too, so a separate product is not always needed.

Semantic search finds results by meaning rather than exact words. It compares embeddings of the query and the documents, so a search for car fault can find vehicle defect. It works well for paraphrased questions but can miss exact codes and part numbers.

Hybrid search runs keyword search and semantic search together and merges the results. Keywords catch exact terms like SOP numbers, while semantic search catches different wording. It is often the best default for RAG over business documents.

Reranking is a second step in search where a more careful model re-scores the top results from a fast first search. It pushes the most relevant passages to the top before they go to the language model. It usually improves RAG answers at a small extra cost.

Cosine similarity measures how closely two vectors point in the same direction. In search it is the usual score for how similar two embeddings, and so two texts, are in meaning. A higher score means more similar.

A knowledge graph stores facts as entities and the relationships between them, such as supplier provides part, part used in device. It makes connected questions easy to answer. It can be combined with RAG so a model follows links, not just similar text.

An ontology is an agreed model of the concepts in a domain and how they relate. A taxonomy is a simpler version that only arranges terms in a hierarchy. Both help systems and people use the same words for the same things.

Chain of thought is when a model writes out intermediate reasoning steps before giving an answer. It often improves results on multi-step problems like calculations and logic. Reasoning models do this internally, so you rarely need to ask for it explicitly.

Few-shot prompting puts a handful of worked examples in the prompt to show the model the pattern you want. It is a quick way to fix format and style without training. Pick examples that cover the tricky cases, not only easy ones.

Zero-shot prompting asks the model to do a task with instructions only and no examples. Modern models handle many tasks this way. If results are inconsistent, adding a few examples is the usual next step.

Prompt chaining splits a job into several smaller model calls where each output feeds the next step. Each step is simpler, easier to test and easier to fix. An example is extract fields, then check them, then draft a summary.

A prompt template is a fixed prompt with placeholders that code fills in for each request, such as the document text or user question. It keeps prompts consistent and lets you version and test them. Templates are usually stored as files beside the code.

entries.q: What is structured output from an LLM?
entries.a: Structured output means the model returns data in a fixed shape, usually JSON that matches a schema you define. Many APIs can enforce the schema so the result always parses. It does not guarantee the values are correct, so you still validate them.

An agentic workflow is a process where a model plans steps, calls tools and acts on the results, rather than answering once. Some steps are fixed in code and some are chosen by the model. More freedom means more power but also more need for limits and logging.

A multi-agent system has several AI agents, each with its own role or tools, working together on a task. One agent often coordinates and hands work to others. It can help with large jobs, but it adds cost and makes failures harder to trace.

entries.q: What is human in the loop?
entries.a: Human in the loop means a person reviews, corrects or approves AI output at defined points before it takes effect. It is standard for high-risk decisions, especially in regulated work. The design should make real review easy, not a click-through.

Grounding means making a model base its answer on specific trusted sources, such as retrieved documents, rather than on memory alone. Grounded answers can cite where each claim came from. It is one of the main ways to reduce hallucinations.

A foundation model is a large model trained on broad data that can be adapted to many tasks. Large language models are the best known kind. Teams build on top of one with prompting, RAG or fine-tuning instead of training from scratch.

entries.q: What is a small language model?
entries.a: A small language model is a language model with far fewer parameters than the largest ones. It is cheaper and faster and can run on modest hardware or devices. It suits narrow, well defined tasks but is weaker at broad reasoning.

A diffusion model generates images by starting from random noise and removing it step by step until a picture appears. It is the main technique behind many text-to-image tools. Similar ideas are used for audio and video.

AGI, artificial general intelligence, is the idea of an AI that can learn and do most intellectual tasks a person can. There is no agreed test for it and opinions differ on how close current systems are. For client work, judge systems on the specific tasks they need to do.

Synthetic data is data generated by software or a model rather than collected from real events. It helps when real data is scarce or sensitive, for tests or demos. It may miss the messy edge cases of real data, so do not rely on it alone for evaluation.

Data drift is when the inputs a model sees in production change from what it was built and tested on. Concept drift is when the relationship between inputs and the right answer changes. Either can quietly lower quality, so production data is monitored over time.

MLOps is the practice of running machine learning models reliably in production. It covers versioning data and models, automated testing and deployment, monitoring and retraining. LLMOps applies the same ideas to prompts and language model apps.

A model registry is a central record of trained models, their versions, metrics and approval status. It shows which version is in production and lets teams roll back. In regulated settings it supports traceability of what was used when.

entries.q: What is red teaming for AI?
entries.a: Red teaming is deliberately trying to make an AI system misbehave, for example leak data, ignore rules or give harmful answers. Findings are fixed before release and turned into test cases. It is a standard part of AI safety and security testing.

entries.q: What is a jailbreak in AI?
entries.a: A jailbreak is a prompt crafted to make a model ignore its safety rules or instructions. It is related to prompt injection but usually comes from the user directly. Defences include model safety training, input and output checks, and limiting what the system can do.

AI governance is the set of policies, roles and controls an organization uses to decide which AI uses are allowed and how they are checked. It covers risk assessment, approvals, documentation, monitoring and accountability. In regulated companies it ties into the existing quality system.

Responsible AI means building and using AI in a way that is fair, safe, transparent, private and accountable. It turns those values into practical checks such as bias testing, human oversight and clear documentation. Most large organizations have a responsible AI policy.

Explainability is how well people can understand why an AI system gave a particular output. It matters when decisions must be justified to users, auditors or regulators. Methods range from showing source documents to feature importance scores.

Bias in AI is when a system gives systematically worse or unfair results for some groups or case types. It usually comes from unbalanced training data or design choices. It is found by testing results split by group, not just overall.

A model card is a short document describing a model: what it is for, how it was trained, how it was evaluated and its known limits. Model providers publish them, and teams can write their own for internal models. It helps reviewers judge if a model fits a use.

entries.q: What is the EU AI Act?
entries.a: The EU AI Act is a European Union law that regulates AI systems by risk level. Some uses are banned, high-risk uses face strict requirements like risk management, documentation and human oversight, and lower-risk uses mainly face transparency duties. AI that is part of a regulated medical device can fall into the high-risk group.

entries.q: What is the NIST AI Risk Management Framework?
entries.a: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework is voluntary guidance from the US National Institute of Standards and Technology for managing AI risks. It is organized around four functions: govern, map, measure and manage. Many companies use it to structure their AI governance.

ISO/IEC 42001 is an international standard for an AI management system. It sets requirements for how an organization governs, risk-assesses and monitors its AI work, in a similar style to ISO 27001 for security. Organizations can be certified against it.

A deepfake is realistic fake audio, image or video made with AI, often showing a real person saying or doing something they did not. Deepfakes are used in fraud, for example faking an executive's voice on a call. Verification steps for payments and approvals help defend against them.

An AI copilot is an assistant built into a tool that helps a person do their work, such as drafting, summarizing or suggesting code. The person stays in control and accepts or edits the suggestions. It is a common first pattern for AI in business software.

Anomaly detection finds data points or events that differ from the normal pattern. It is used for fraud, equipment faults and unusual process readings. Flagged items still need a person or rule to decide if they matter.

A recommendation system suggests items a user is likely to want, based on their past behaviour and that of similar users. Shops and streaming services are common examples. In business tools it can suggest similar past cases or relevant documents.

AI literacy is a basic working understanding of what AI can and cannot do, how to use it safely and how to check its output. It helps staff avoid both blind trust and blanket refusal. The EU AI Act asks organizations using AI to support AI literacy for their staff.

Object-oriented programming, OOP, organizes code around objects that bundle data with the functions that act on it. Its main ideas are classes, encapsulation, inheritance and polymorphism. Java, C# and Python all support it.

entries.q: What is a class in programming?
entries.a: A class is a blueprint that defines what data an object holds and what it can do. For example, a Batch class might hold a batch number and status and have a method to release it. Each actual batch you create from it is an object.

entries.q: What is an object in programming?
entries.a: An object is one concrete thing created from a class, with its own data. If Batch is the class, batch B-1001 is an object. In JavaScript, object also means a simple set of key and value pairs.

entries.q: What is a method in programming?
entries.a: A method is a function that belongs to a class or object and works on its data. You call it on the object, like batch.release(). It is the same idea as a function, just attached to an object.

Inheritance lets one class reuse and extend another. A child class gets the parent's data and methods and can add or change some. Overusing it makes code hard to follow, so many teams prefer composition.

Encapsulation means keeping an object's internal data hidden and only allowing changes through its own methods. This protects the data from being set to invalid values. It also lets you change the inside without breaking code that uses it.

Polymorphism means different types can be used through the same interface, each doing its own version of the action. For example, both a PDF exporter and a CSV exporter can have an export method. Calling code does not need to know which one it has.

entries.q: What is a function in programming?
entries.a: A function is a named block of code that takes inputs, does one job and usually returns a result. Functions let you reuse logic and test it in isolation. Good functions are short and do one clear thing.
A variable is a name that refers to a value stored in memory, such as count = 5. You use the name to read or change the value later. Clear variable names make code much easier to read.

A data type tells the program what kind of value something is and what you can do with it. Common types are integer, decimal number, text string, boolean and date. Mixing types up is a common source of bugs, such as adding a number to text.

entries.q: What is a string in programming?
entries.a: A string is a piece of text, a sequence of characters such as a name or a sentence. Numbers stored as strings do not add up like numbers, which often causes bugs in imported data. Most languages put strings in quotes.
A boolean is a value that is either true or false. It is used for yes or no decisions in code, such as is_released. Conditions in if statements evaluate to booleans.

Null means no value at all, which is different from zero or an empty text. Python calls it None and JavaScript has both null and undefined. Forgetting to handle null values is one of the most common causes of crashes.

entries.q: What is an array or list?
entries.a: An array or list is an ordered collection of values that you can access by position, starting at zero in most languages. It is used for things like a list of batch numbers. You can loop over it, add to it and sort it.

entries.q: What is a dictionary or hash map?
entries.a: A dictionary, also called a hash map or map, stores values by key, such as a part number pointing to its description. Looking up a value by key is very fast. JSON objects map naturally to dictionaries.

entries.q: What is a loop in programming?
entries.a: A loop repeats a block of code, either for each item in a collection or while a condition stays true. For example, loop over every row in a file and check it. Watch out for loops that never end.

A conditional runs different code depending on whether something is true, using if, else and similar keywords. It is how programs make decisions. Business rules in code are mostly made of conditionals.

Recursion is when a function calls itself on a smaller part of the problem until it reaches a simple base case. It suits tree-shaped data such as folders or a bill of materials. Without a correct base case it never stops and crashes.

entries.q: What is an exception in programming?
entries.a: An exception is an error raised while a program runs, such as a missing file or a failed network call. Code can catch it and handle it, for example retry or log a clear message. Unhandled exceptions stop the program.

A stack trace is the list of function calls that were running when an error happened. It shows the file and line where the error came from and how the code got there. Read it from the most specific line in your own code.
A REST API exposes data as resources at URLs and uses standard HTTP methods like GET, POST, PUT and DELETE on them. Responses are usually JSON. It is the most common style of web API.

GraphQL is an API style where the client sends a query describing exactly which fields it wants, and gets back just that data. It uses a single endpoint and a typed schema. It reduces over-fetching but is more complex to secure and cache than REST.

gRPC is a fast API framework where a client calls functions on a remote server as if they were local. It uses Protocol Buffers, a compact binary format, and a strict contract file. It is popular for service to service calls inside a system.

A webhook is when one system calls a URL you provide whenever an event happens, instead of you checking repeatedly. For example, a payment system calls your endpoint when a payment succeeds. Your endpoint must verify the call is genuine and handle repeats safely.

SOAP is an older web service protocol that sends XML messages with a strict contract described in a WSDL file. It is still common in enterprise and legacy systems. New integrations usually use REST, but you will meet SOAP in older ERP and quality systems.
An endpoint is a specific URL and method where an API accepts requests, such as GET /batches/123. Each endpoint does one job. API documentation lists the endpoints, inputs and outputs.

entries.q: What are HTTP methods like GET and POST?
entries.a: HTTP methods tell the server what action you want. GET reads data, POST creates or submits, PUT or PATCH updates, and DELETE removes. GET requests should not change anything on the server.

OpenAPI is a standard format for describing a REST API: its endpoints, inputs, outputs and authentication. Tools can turn the description into documentation, test clients and code. Swagger is the older name and a set of tools around it.

An API gateway is a single entry point that sits in front of backend services and handles common jobs like authentication, rate limits, logging and routing. Clients call the gateway instead of each service. Cloud providers offer managed gateways.

API versioning lets an API change without breaking existing users, for example by putting v1 or v2 in the URL. Old clients keep using the old version while new ones move. It matters when other teams depend on your API.

entries.q: What is pagination in an API?
entries.a: Pagination splits a large result into pages so an API returns a limited number of records per call. You follow a page number or a next cursor to get the rest. Forgetting to page through results is a common reason for missing data.

HTML, hypertext markup language, describes the structure and content of a web page using tags like headings, paragraphs, links and forms. The browser reads it to build the page. CSS styles it and JavaScript makes it interactive.
CSS, cascading style sheets, controls how a web page looks: colours, fonts, spacing and layout. It is kept separate from the HTML content. Frameworks like Tailwind provide ready-made styles.

The DOM, document object model, is the browser's live tree of the page's elements built from the HTML. JavaScript reads and changes the DOM to update what you see without reloading. Browser automation tools also work through the DOM.

A single-page application loads one page and then updates parts of it with JavaScript as the user moves around, instead of loading new pages from the server. React, Vue and Angular are common ways to build them. They feel fast but need extra care for search engines and first load.

Responsive design makes a web page adapt its layout to the screen size, from phone to large monitor. It uses flexible layouts and CSS rules that change at different widths. Shop floor tablets and phones make this matter for business tools.

Web accessibility means building software that people with disabilities can use, for example with screen readers, keyboard only or low vision. WCAG is the main guideline. Many organizations require it by policy or law.

A cookie is a small piece of data a website stores in the browser and sends back on each request. A session uses a cookie to remember that a user is logged in. Session cookies should be secure and expire.

A JWT, JSON web token, is a signed token that carries claims such as who the user is and when the token expires. Services check the signature to trust it without calling the login server. Anyone can read its contents, so never put secrets in it.

A regular expression, or regex, is a compact pattern for finding or checking text, such as a lot number format or an email address. It is powerful but hard to read, so test each pattern on real examples. Most languages and editors support it.

A runtime is the environment that runs your code and provides basic services like memory and input and output. Node.js is a JavaScript runtime and the JVM is Java's runtime. Runtime also means the time while a program is running, as in a runtime error.

entries.q: What is the difference between a library and a framework?
entries.a: A library is code you call when you need it, like a date or PDF library. A framework calls your code: it sets the structure and you fill in the parts, like Django or React. Frameworks speed up work but shape how you build.

A dependency is outside code your project needs to run, such as a library installed with pip or npm. Dependencies save time but bring risks like security flaws and breaking updates. Pin versions and keep a list so builds are repeatable.

entries.q: What is a module in programming?
entries.a: A module is a file or unit of code that groups related functions and classes, which other code can import. Splitting code into modules keeps it organized. In Python each .py file is a module.
Semantic versioning numbers releases as major.minor.patch, such as 2.4.1. A major bump means breaking changes, minor adds features safely and patch fixes bugs. It tells users how risky an upgrade is.

entries.q: What is an open source license?
entries.a: An open source license is the legal terms that let you use, change and share someone's code. Permissive licenses like MIT and Apache 2.0 allow most uses, while copyleft licenses like GPL can require you to share your changes. Check licenses before shipping code to a client.

An IDE, integrated development environment, is an application for writing code with tools like autocomplete, debugging and Git built in. VS Code, IntelliJ and PyCharm are common examples. Many now include AI coding assistants.
A CLI, command line interface, is a program you use by typing commands in a terminal instead of clicking. Git, Docker and cloud tools all have CLIs. CLIs are easy to script and automate.

An environment variable is a named setting provided to a program by its environment, such as a database URL or API key. It keeps settings and secrets out of the code. A .env file is a common way to set them locally, and it must not be committed.

YAML is a human-friendly text format for configuration, using indentation instead of brackets. It is used for CI pipelines, Kubernetes and many tools. Indentation mistakes are the most common YAML error.

XML, extensible markup language, stores data using nested tags, similar to HTML. It is verbose but strict and is common in older enterprise systems, SOAP services and regulatory submissions. Newer APIs mostly use JSON.

Character encoding is how text is stored as bytes. UTF-8 is the modern standard and can represent almost every language. Reading a file with the wrong encoding produces garbled characters, a common problem with exported CSV files.
A cron job is a task scheduled to run automatically at set times, such as every night at 2am. The name comes from the Unix cron scheduler. Cloud platforms offer similar scheduled triggers.

An algorithm is a clear set of steps to solve a problem, such as sorting a list or finding the shortest route. Code is an algorithm written in a programming language. Different algorithms for the same job can differ a lot in speed.

Big O notation describes how the time or memory of an algorithm grows as the input grows. O(n) grows in step with the input, while O(n squared) gets slow quickly on large data. It helps you spot code that will not scale.

A data structure is a way of organizing data in memory so certain operations are efficient. Lists, dictionaries, sets, queues and trees are common ones. Picking the right one often matters more than clever code.

A debugger is a tool that lets you pause a running program at a breakpoint and inspect variables line by line. It shows exactly what the code is doing instead of guessing. Most IDEs have one built in.

Debugging is finding and fixing the cause of wrong behaviour in software. A good approach is to reproduce the problem, narrow down where it happens, form a guess, test it, then fix and add a test. Reading logs and error messages comes first.
A unit test checks one small piece of code, like a single function, in isolation. Unit tests run fast and catch bugs early when code changes. Tools like pytest and Jest run them automatically.

An integration test checks that several parts work together, such as your code with a real database or API. It catches problems unit tests miss, like wrong field names between systems. It is slower, so you usually have fewer of them.

An end-to-end test runs a whole user journey through the real system, often by driving a browser. It confirms the pieces work together from the user's view. These tests are slow and fragile, so keep them for the key paths.

Regression testing re-runs existing tests after a change to make sure nothing that used to work is now broken. In software, a regression is a bug in something that worked before. Automated test suites in CI do this on every change.

Test-driven development, TDD, means writing a failing test first, then the code to make it pass, then cleaning up. It keeps code testable and gives quick feedback. Many teams use it for core logic rather than everything.
Test coverage is the share of code lines or branches that run during tests. Low coverage shows untested areas. High coverage does not prove the tests check the right things.

entries.q: What is a mock in testing?
entries.a: A mock is a fake version of a dependency, such as an API or database, used in tests. It returns set answers so tests run fast and repeatably without the real system. Too much mocking can hide integration problems.

Refactoring is changing the structure of code to make it cleaner or easier to change, without changing what it does. Tests make it safe because they show nothing broke. Small, frequent refactors are better than big rewrites.

A code review is when another developer reads a change before it is merged, looking for bugs, risks and clarity. It spreads knowledge and catches problems early. In regulated work it can also be a documented approval step.

Technical debt is the future cost of shortcuts taken now, like skipped tests or quick hacks. Like money debt, it is sometimes worth taking on but grows if ignored. Teams pay it down by refactoring and fixing the worst spots.

A linter is a tool that checks code for likely bugs and style problems without running it. A formatter rewrites code into a consistent style. Both are usually run automatically in the editor and in CI.

Static analysis examines source code without running it to find bugs, security flaws and bad patterns. Security-focused static analysis is called SAST. It runs in CI and flags issues before code ships.

Design patterns are proven, named solutions to common coding problems, such as factory, observer or adapter. They give developers a shared vocabulary. Use them when they fit the problem, not for their own sake.

MVC, model view controller, is a pattern that splits an application into data and rules (model), what the user sees (view) and the logic connecting them (controller). It keeps code organized. Many web frameworks follow it.

Asynchronous programming lets code start a slow task, like a network call, and do other work while waiting instead of blocking. Keywords like async and await make it readable. It is how one program can handle many API calls at once.

Concurrency is a program handling several tasks at overlapping times. Parallelism is actually running them at the same moment on multiple cores. Both speed up work but bring bugs like race conditions.
A thread is a single sequence of work inside a program. A process can run several threads that share memory. Sharing memory is fast but needs care so threads do not overwrite each other's data.

A race condition is a bug where the result depends on the timing of two tasks touching the same data. For example, two users approving the same record at once could both succeed. Locks and database transactions prevent it.

A deadlock is when two tasks each wait for something the other holds, so neither can continue. It shows up in threads and in databases. Fixes include always taking locks in the same order and using timeouts.

Microservices split an application into small services that each own one job and talk over APIs. Teams can deploy and scale them separately. The cost is more moving parts, network calls and monitoring.
A monolith is an application built and deployed as one unit. It is simpler to build, test and run, which suits small teams and early products. It becomes harder to change as it grows very large.

In event-driven architecture, systems publish events like batch released, and other systems react to them. Producers and consumers do not need to know about each other. It decouples systems but makes the full flow harder to trace.

Publish-subscribe is a messaging pattern where senders publish messages to a topic and every subscriber to that topic gets a copy. It lets one event reach many systems. Cloud services and tools like Kafka provide it.

Caching stores the result of slow work, like a database query or API call, so the next request can reuse it quickly. It improves speed and lowers cost. The hard part is knowing when cached data is out of date.

An ORM, object-relational mapper, lets code work with database rows as objects instead of writing raw SQL. SQLAlchemy and Prisma are examples. It speeds up development but can produce slow queries if you do not check them.

CRUD stands for create, read, update and delete, the four basic operations on stored data. Many business apps are mostly CRUD screens over a database. REST APIs map them to POST, GET, PUT or PATCH, and DELETE.

The SDLC, software development life cycle, is the set of stages software goes through: requirements, design, build, test, release and maintenance. Agile and waterfall are different ways of running it. Regulated industries document each stage.

Low-code and no-code platforms let people build apps and workflows with visual tools and little or no hand-written code. They are fast for simple, standard needs. Complex logic, testing and version control can be harder than in code.

RPA, robotic process automation, uses software bots that click and type through applications the way a person would. It automates repetitive tasks in systems without good APIs. Bots break when screens change, so they need maintenance.

Backward compatibility means a new version still works with things built for the old version. A breaking change is one that is not compatible and forces users to update. APIs and file formats should avoid breaking changes or version them clearly.

Localhost is the name a computer uses for itself, usually at address 127.0.0.1. Running an app on localhost means it is only reachable from your own machine. It is the normal place to develop and test.

A schema is the defined structure of data: which tables or fields exist, their types and how they relate. In a database it is the set of table definitions. A JSON schema does the same for JSON documents.

Metadata is data that describes other data, such as a file's author, created date, version or document type. It makes data easier to find, filter and trust. In RAG, metadata like site or document status is used to filter search results.

Master data is the core shared business records that many processes use, such as materials, products, suppliers, customers and sites. Master data management, MDM, keeps one trusted golden record for each. Bad master data causes errors in every system that uses it.

Reference data is the fixed lists of allowed values other data points to, such as country codes, units of measure or defect categories. It changes rarely and is often shared across systems. Keeping it consistent makes reporting line up.

Transactional data records business events, such as orders, batch steps, test results or complaints. It grows constantly and points to master data like product and supplier. Most analytics are built from it.

entries.q: What is the difference between structured and unstructured data?
entries.a: Structured data fits neatly into rows and columns, like a database table. Unstructured data has no fixed shape, like emails, PDFs, images and audio. Semi-structured data such as JSON sits in between. LLMs are especially useful for turning unstructured data into structured fields.

A data lake is cheap storage that holds large amounts of raw data in its original format, structured or not. Data is shaped when it is read rather than when it is loaded. Without good cataloguing it can become a swamp nobody trusts.

A lakehouse combines a data lake's cheap, flexible storage with data warehouse features like tables, transactions and fast SQL. Open table formats such as Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg make this possible. Databricks popularized the term.

A data mart is a smaller, focused part of a data warehouse built for one team or subject, such as quality or supply chain. It holds just the tables that team needs in a simple shape. It makes reporting faster and easier for that group.

ELT, extract load transform, copies raw data into the target platform first and transforms it there using the platform's own compute. It is the common pattern with modern cloud warehouses. ETL transforms before loading instead.

A data pipeline is a set of automated steps that moves data from sources, cleans and changes it, and loads it where it is needed. It usually runs on a schedule or on events. Pipelines need monitoring so failures and bad data are caught.

entries.q: What is a workflow orchestrator for data?
entries.a: A workflow orchestrator schedules and runs the steps of data pipelines in the right order and retries failures. Apache Airflow is a well known one, which defines workflows as DAGs, graphs of tasks. It gives one place to see what ran and what failed.

Change data capture, CDC, detects inserts, updates and deletes in a source database and passes only those changes on. It keeps copies up to date without reloading everything. It is often done by reading the database log.

Big data means datasets too large, fast or varied for a single normal database or computer to handle well. It is often described by volume, velocity and variety. Tools like Spark spread the work across many machines.
Apache Spark is an engine for processing large data across a cluster of machines. You write code in Python, SQL or Scala and Spark splits the work. It underpins platforms like Databricks.

Apache Kafka is a platform for streaming events in real time. Producers write events to topics and many consumers read them, at their own pace. It is used to move data between systems as things happen.

Databricks and Snowflake are popular cloud data platforms. Databricks grew from Spark and the lakehouse idea and is strong for data engineering and machine learning. Snowflake grew as a cloud data warehouse and is strong for SQL analytics. Both now overlap a lot.

Parquet is a file format that stores data by column and compresses it well. Analytical queries read only the columns they need, so they are much faster than with CSV. It is the standard file format in data lakes.

entries.q: What is the difference between OLTP and OLAP?
entries.a: OLTP, online transaction processing, systems handle many small reads and writes for daily operations, like an ERP. OLAP, online analytical processing, systems handle large queries for reporting and analysis, like a data warehouse. Running heavy reports on an OLTP system can slow down operations.

A star schema is a data warehouse design with a central fact table of events or measures, linked to dimension tables that describe them, such as date, product and site. It makes reporting queries simple and fast. Drawn out, it looks like a star.

Data modeling is designing how data is organized: the entities, their fields and how they relate. It usually goes from a conceptual model to a logical and then a physical database design. Good models make data easier to trust and query.

An ERD, entity relationship diagram, is a picture of the tables or entities in a system and how they relate, such as one supplier to many parts. It is the usual way to communicate a database design. It helps spot missing links before building.

Normalization is designing tables so each fact is stored in one place, which avoids duplicate and conflicting data. For example, supplier details live in a supplier table, not copied into every order. It is standard for transactional databases.

Denormalization deliberately copies data into fewer, wider tables so reads are faster and simpler. It is common in data warehouses and reporting. The trade-off is more storage and the risk of copies getting out of sync.

A database transaction groups several changes so they either all succeed or all fail together. If anything goes wrong, the database rolls back to how it was. For example, moving stock between two locations should never leave it in neither.

ACID stands for atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability, the guarantees a reliable database gives transactions. In short, changes are all or nothing, rules are kept, parallel work does not clash and saved data survives crashes. Relational databases like PostgreSQL are ACID.

A relational database stores data in tables of rows and columns, linked by keys, and is queried with SQL. PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle and MySQL are common ones. It is the default choice for business records.

NoSQL is a broad name for databases that do not use the classic table model, such as document, key-value, wide-column and graph databases. They suit flexible or very high scale data. Many give up some consistency guarantees in exchange.

A document database stores records as JSON-like documents, so each record can have its own nested structure. MongoDB is a well known example. It suits data whose shape varies, but joins across documents are harder.
A key-value store saves values under unique keys and fetches them very fast by key. It is used for caches, sessions and settings. Redis is a common example.
A graph database stores data as nodes and the relationships between them. It is fast for connected questions, like which devices use parts from this supplier lot. Neo4j is a common example.

Time series data is a sequence of measurements taken over time, such as temperature every minute from a cleanroom. Special time series databases store and query it efficiently. It is used for monitoring, trends and forecasting.
A view is a saved query that behaves like a table. It hides complex joins and can limit which columns users see. A materialized view stores the results for speed and must be refreshed.

A stored procedure is a named block of SQL logic saved inside the database and run on request. It keeps some business logic close to the data. Logic hidden in procedures can be hard to test and version, so document it.

Replication keeps copies of a database on other servers, updated from the main one. Replicas can take read load and step in if the main server fails. Some replication has a short delay, so replicas may be slightly behind.
Partitioning splits a large table into parts, often by date, so queries scan less data. Sharding spreads data across several separate servers. Both help scale, and sharding adds a lot of complexity.
Business intelligence, BI, is turning business data into reports and dashboards people use to make decisions. Power BI, Tableau and Looker are common tools. BI usually reads from a data warehouse.

A dashboard is a single screen of charts and numbers that shows the current state of key measures. A good one answers a specific set of questions for a specific audience. Too many charts make it hard to see what matters.

A KPI, key performance indicator, is a measure that shows whether a team or process is meeting an important goal, such as on-time release rate or complaint closure time. Each KPI needs a clear definition, data source and target. Only a few measures should be KPIs.

entries.q: What are descriptive, diagnostic, predictive and prescriptive analytics?
entries.a: Descriptive analytics says what happened, diagnostic says why, predictive estimates what will happen and prescriptive suggests what to do. Each step needs more data and more trust in the model. Most organizations do mostly descriptive work.

Data visualization is showing data as charts, maps or graphics so patterns are easy to see. The right chart depends on the question, such as a line for trends and bars for comparing groups. Clear labels matter more than decoration.

A semantic layer sits between raw data and reporting tools and defines business terms and metrics once, such as what counts as a late batch. Every report then uses the same definition. It stops different dashboards showing different numbers for the same thing.

Data governance is the set of roles, policies and processes that decide who owns data, who can use it and how its quality is kept. It makes data trustworthy and compliant. Without it, nobody is sure which number is right.

entries.q: What are a data owner and a data steward?
entries.a: A data owner is the business person accountable for a set of data, deciding who can access it and how it is used. A data steward looks after it day to day, fixing quality issues and keeping definitions up to date. IT usually acts as custodian, running the systems that store it.

Data lineage traces where data came from, what happened to it and where it went. It answers which source fed this number in the report. It is vital for debugging, audits and impact analysis before changes.

A data catalog is a searchable inventory of an organization's datasets with descriptions, owners and lineage. It helps people find data and know if they can trust it. Tools like Unity Catalog and Purview provide one.
A data dictionary lists each field in a dataset with its meaning, type, allowed values and source. A business glossary does the same for business terms. Both stop people guessing what a column means.

entries.q: What are the dimensions of data quality?
entries.a: Data quality is usually judged on dimensions such as accuracy, completeness, consistency, timeliness, validity and uniqueness. Each one can be measured with simple checks, like the share of missing values. Agree which dimensions matter for the use case before measuring.

Data profiling is examining a dataset to understand its contents: value ranges, null counts, distinct values and odd patterns. It is the first thing to do with new client data. It shows quality problems before you build on them.

Deduplication finds and merges records that refer to the same real thing, such as one supplier entered three ways. Exact matches are easy, while near matches need fuzzy rules or models. It is a core part of master data cleanup.

Sampling is studying a subset of data instead of all of it. A random sample gives every item an equal chance, and a stratified sample takes items from each group in proportion. A biased sample gives misleading conclusions.

An outlier is a value far from the rest of the data. It might be a real rare event or a data entry error. Investigate before removing it, because in quality data outliers are often the most important points.

A data mesh is an approach where each business domain owns and publishes its own data as a product, instead of one central team owning everything. A shared platform and standards keep it consistent. It suits large organizations with many data teams.

A data contract is an agreement between a data producer and its consumers on the schema, meaning and quality of a dataset. Changes that break it must be agreed first. It prevents pipelines breaking silently when a source changes.

DevOps is a way of working where development and operations share responsibility for building, releasing and running software. It relies on automation like CI/CD, infrastructure as code and monitoring. The aim is small, frequent, safe releases.

SRE, site reliability engineering, applies software engineering to running systems reliably. SRE teams set reliability targets, automate operations work and lead incident response. It started at Google and is now widely used.

Platform engineering builds an internal platform of shared tools, templates and self-service infrastructure so product teams can ship without reinventing setup. It reduces repeated work and enforces good defaults. It grew out of DevOps.

An SLA, service level agreement, is a commitment to a customer about service levels, such as availability or support response times. In a contract it usually says what happens if the target is missed, often service credits. Internal teams use SLOs to stay safely above the SLA.

An SLO, service level objective, is an internal target for how reliable a service should be, such as 99.9 percent of requests succeed over 30 days as an example. It is measured with SLIs. It is set tighter than any SLA so problems are fixed before customers are owed anything.

An SLI, service level indicator, is the actual measured value of a reliability aspect, such as the share of successful requests or the share of requests served under a time limit. SLOs are targets set on SLIs. Pick SLIs that reflect what users feel.

An error budget is the amount of failure an SLO allows, for example the small share of requests that may fail in a month. While budget remains, the team can ship changes quickly. When it runs out, the focus shifts to reliability.

entries.q: What is an incident in IT operations?
entries.a: An incident is an unplanned event that disrupts or degrades a service, like an outage or a security alert. Incident management is the process to detect it, restore service quickly and communicate. Severity levels decide how urgent the response is.

A postmortem is a written review after an incident covering what happened, the impact, the causes and the actions to prevent a repeat. Good postmortems are blameless, focusing on systems rather than people. Actions should be tracked to closure.
On-call means an engineer is responsible for responding to alerts for a set period, including outside working hours. Teams share it on a rotation. Good alerts and runbooks keep on-call bearable.

A runbook is a step-by-step guide for a known operational task or alert, such as restarting a stuck job or rotating a key. It lets anyone on-call act quickly and consistently. Some steps can be automated over time.

Monitoring collects and watches measures like errors, latency and resource use. Alerting notifies people when a measure crosses a threshold that needs action. Alerts should be few, meaningful and tied to a runbook.

Availability is the share of time a service is working for users, often written as a percentage like 99.9. Each extra nine allows much less downtime and costs more to achieve. Match the target to what the business really needs.

MTTR is mean time to recovery or repair, the average time to restore service after a failure. MTBF, mean time between failures, is the average time a system runs between failures. Lower MTTR and higher MTBF both mean better reliability.

DORA metrics are four widely used measures of software delivery: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service. They come from the DevOps Research and Assessment program. They balance speed against stability.

In SRE, toil is manual, repetitive operations work that could be automated and does not add lasting value, like restarting the same job each week. Teams track it and automate it away. Too much toil burns people out.

A load balancer spreads incoming requests across several servers so no single one is overloaded. It also stops sending traffic to servers that fail health checks. It is a basic building block of high availability.
A reverse proxy is a server that receives requests on behalf of backend servers and forwards them. It can handle TLS, caching, compression and routing. Nginx is a common example.

A CDN, content delivery network, is a network of servers around the world that cache and serve content close to users. It makes sites faster and absorbs traffic spikes and some attacks. Static files and images are typical CDN content.

Edge computing runs processing close to where data is created, such as on factory equipment or at a nearby network location, instead of in a central cloud. It lowers latency and can keep data on site. It is common in manufacturing and IoT.

Autoscaling automatically adds or removes servers or containers based on load. It keeps performance steady during peaks and saves money when quiet. Limits should be set so a bug cannot scale up costs without bound.

entries.q: What is the difference between vertical and horizontal scaling?
entries.a: Vertical scaling means giving one machine more CPU or memory. Horizontal scaling means adding more machines and sharing the load. Horizontal scaling goes further but needs the application to be designed for it.

Capacity planning is estimating how much compute, storage and network a system will need and making sure it is there in time. It uses current usage, expected growth and peak patterns. For AI apps it includes model rate limits and token budgets.

A virtual machine, VM, is a software computer with its own operating system running on shared physical hardware. Cloud servers are usually VMs. They are heavier than containers but give stronger isolation.

A container registry stores and distributes container images, much like a library for built applications. CI pushes new images there and servers pull them to run. Examples include Docker Hub and the registries from each cloud provider.

Container orchestration automatically runs, places, scales, restarts and connects containers across many machines. Kubernetes is the most widely used orchestrator. It is powerful but adds complexity small projects may not need.

Helm is a package manager for Kubernetes. A Helm chart bundles all the configuration needed to deploy an application, with settings you can change per environment. It makes repeatable Kubernetes deployments easier.

A service mesh is a layer that handles communication between services, adding encryption, retries, routing and metrics without changing app code. It usually works through small proxy sidecars next to each service. Istio and Linkerd are examples.

entries.q: What is configuration management in IT?
entries.a: Configuration management keeps servers and software set up in a known, consistent state using code instead of manual changes. Tools like Ansible, Puppet and Chef apply the settings. In regulated work, configuration management also means tracking approved versions of every component.

GitOps is a way of running infrastructure and deployments where the desired state lives in a Git repository and an automated agent makes the live system match it. Every change goes through a pull request. It gives an audit trail and easy rollback.
Immutable infrastructure means servers are never changed after they are deployed. To update, you build a new image and replace the old servers. This avoids drift and makes environments repeatable.

A build artifact is the output of a build, such as a container image, a package or a compiled file, that gets deployed. Storing versioned artifacts means you deploy exactly what was tested. Artifact repositories keep them.

A blue-green deployment runs two identical environments: blue is live and green gets the new version. After checks, traffic switches to green, and blue stays ready for instant rollback. It reduces downtime and risk but needs double resources during the switch.

A canary release sends a new version to a small share of users first and watches errors and metrics. If all is well, the share grows until everyone is on it. If not, traffic goes back to the old version with little impact.

A rolling deployment replaces old instances with new ones a few at a time, so the service stays up. It is the default in Kubernetes. Both versions run together for a while, so they must be compatible.

A feature flag is a switch in configuration that turns a feature on or off without redeploying. It lets teams ship code early, test with some users and turn things off fast. Old flags should be removed so code does not get messy.

A rollback returns a system to the last known good version after a bad release. It should be quick, rehearsed and include config and prompt changes, not just code. Database changes make rollback harder, so plan them carefully.

High availability means designing a system to keep running when parts fail, by removing single points of failure. Typical steps are multiple servers, multiple zones and automatic failover. The more availability you need, the more it costs.

Fault tolerance is a system's ability to keep working correctly when a component fails. Graceful degradation means it keeps working with reduced features rather than failing completely. Retries, timeouts and fallbacks are common tools.

Redundancy means having spare components ready, such as a second database server. Failover is switching to the spare when the main one fails, ideally automatically. Failover should be tested, not assumed.

Disaster recovery is the plan and setup for restoring systems and data after a major failure, such as losing a whole data centre or region. It defines priorities, steps and recovery targets. It must be tested regularly to be trusted.

Business continuity is keeping critical business functions running during and after a disruption, including people, sites and suppliers, not only IT. Disaster recovery is the IT part of it. ISO 22301 is the standard for it.

A backup is a copy of data kept separately so it can be restored after loss, corruption or attack. Good practice keeps several copies, on different media, with at least one off site or offline. A backup only counts once a restore has been tested.

RPO, recovery point objective, is how much data you can afford to lose, measured as time back to the last good copy. RTO, recovery time objective, is how long you can afford to be down. Both drive how backups and failover are designed.

AWS, Amazon Web Services, is Amazon's cloud platform and the largest public cloud provider. It offers hundreds of services, from servers and storage to databases and AI models through Amazon Bedrock. Many enterprises run some or all of their systems there.

Microsoft Azure is Microsoft's cloud platform. It is popular with enterprises already using Microsoft products like Office 365, Active Directory and SQL Server. It offers AI models through Azure AI services.

Google Cloud, or GCP, is Google's cloud platform. It is known for data and analytics services like BigQuery and for AI through Vertex AI. Like AWS and Azure, it offers compute, storage, networking and databases.

entries.q: What are multi-cloud and hybrid cloud?
entries.a: Multi-cloud means using more than one public cloud provider. Hybrid cloud means combining public cloud with on-premises systems. Both are common in large companies and add work for networking, security and skills.

entries.q: What is a managed service in the cloud?
entries.a: A managed service is a cloud offering where the provider runs the infrastructure, patching and backups, and you just use it, such as a managed database. It saves operations work at a higher price. You still own your data and configuration.

Object storage keeps files as objects in buckets, each with a key and metadata, accessed over an API. Amazon S3 and Azure Blob Storage are examples. It is cheap and huge, and it is the usual home for documents, backups and data lake files.

entries.q: What are block and file storage?
entries.a: Block storage works like a raw disk attached to a server and suits databases. File storage is a shared folder many servers can use. Object storage is the third main type, accessed over an API.

Multi-tenant means one copy of an application serves many customers, with each customer's data kept separate. It is how most SaaS works and keeps costs low. Single-tenant gives each customer their own copy, for more isolation at more cost.

A cold start is the delay when a serverless function or container must start up before handling a request. Later requests are faster while it stays warm. It matters for user-facing endpoints that need quick responses.

Cloud cost optimisation is reducing cloud spend without hurting the service. Common steps are rightsizing servers, turning off idle resources, using commitment discounts and picking cheaper storage tiers. For AI apps, model choice and token use are often the biggest levers.

FinOps is the practice of managing cloud spending as a shared job between engineering, finance and business teams. It brings cost visibility, budgets, tagging and regular review of waste. The aim is to spend on what gives value, not simply to spend less.

entries.q: What are reserved and spot instances?
entries.a: On-demand cloud servers are paid by the hour with no commitment. Reserved instances or savings plans give a discount for committing to usage over time. Spot instances use spare capacity very cheaply but can be taken back at short notice.

ITSM, IT service management, is how an IT organization delivers and supports services, through processes like incident, problem, change and request management. ITIL is the best known framework of ITSM practices. ServiceNow is a common ITSM tool.

entries.q: What is a change advisory board?
entries.a: A change advisory board, CAB, is a group that reviews and approves significant changes to IT systems before they go live. It weighs risk, timing and rollback plans. Many organizations now automate approval for low-risk standard changes.

entries.q: What is problem management in IT?
entries.a: In ITSM, a problem is the underlying cause of one or more incidents. Incident management restores service quickly, while problem management finds and removes the cause. A known error is a problem with a documented cause and workaround.
Chaos engineering deliberately injects failures, like stopping a server, to see if a system copes as expected. It finds weak points before real outages do. It starts small and in safe environments.

Shift left means doing testing, security and quality checks earlier in development rather than at the end. Problems found early are cheaper to fix. Running scans and tests in CI on every change is a typical example.

A health check is a simple test, often an endpoint like /health, that tells a load balancer or orchestrator whether a service is working. Unhealthy instances get restarted or taken out of traffic. A readiness check confirms the service is ready to take requests.

A staging environment is a copy of production used for final testing before release. It should match production closely in configuration and data shape. Bugs that only show up in production often come from staging being too different.

Zero trust is a security approach where no user or device is trusted just because it is inside the company network. Every request is checked for identity, device health and permission. It replaces the old idea of a trusted internal network behind a firewall.

Defense in depth means using several independent layers of security so one failure does not expose everything. For example, MFA, network limits, encryption and logging together. Attackers then need to beat many controls, not one.

The attack surface is every point where an attacker could try to get in, such as public endpoints, open ports, user accounts and third-party integrations. An attack vector is a specific path they use. Reducing the attack surface is one of the most effective security steps.

Threat modeling is a structured look at a system's design to find what could be attacked, by whom and how, and what controls to add. STRIDE is a common checklist of threat types. It is done early, when design changes are still cheap.

Phishing is a fake message, usually an email, that tricks someone into clicking a link, opening a file or giving away credentials. Spear phishing targets a specific person with tailored details. Training, MFA and email filters reduce the risk.

Social engineering is manipulating people into breaking security, for example by pretending to be IT support or a senior manager. It targets trust and urgency rather than technology. Verification steps and awareness training are the main defences.

Malware is any software designed to harm, spy on or take control of a system. Viruses, worms, trojans, spyware and ransomware are all malware. It usually arrives through phishing, bad downloads or unpatched systems.

Ransomware is malware that encrypts an organization's data and demands payment to unlock it, often also threatening to leak stolen data. It can stop manufacturing and hospitals. Offline backups, patching and MFA are key defences.

A DDoS, distributed denial of service, attack floods a service with traffic from many machines so real users cannot reach it. Defences include CDNs, cloud DDoS protection and rate limiting. It disrupts service but does not by itself steal data.

entries.q: What is a brute force attack?
entries.a: A brute force attack tries many passwords until one works. Credential stuffing reuses usernames and passwords leaked from other sites. MFA, account lockouts and unique passwords stop most of these attacks.
A man-in-the-middle attack is when someone secretly sits between two parties and reads or changes their traffic. Public Wi-Fi is a common setting. TLS with proper certificate checks prevents it.

Spoofing is faking an identity, such as a sender email address, a caller ID or an IP address, to look trustworthy. Email standards like SPF, DKIM and DMARC help detect spoofed mail. Always verify unusual requests through a separate channel.

An insider threat is a risk that comes from people with legitimate access, such as staff or contractors, whether by malice or mistake. Least privilege, logging and offboarding processes limit the damage. Many data leaks are accidental.

entries.q: What is a software supply chain attack?
entries.a: A software supply chain attack compromises something you trust, such as a library, build tool or vendor update, to reach many victims at once. Defences include pinning dependencies, checking signatures and keeping an SBOM. It is a growing risk for every project using open source.

A zero-day is a vulnerability that attackers know about before the vendor has a fix. There is no patch yet, so defence relies on other layers like monitoring and limiting access. Once a patch is out, it should be applied quickly.

A vulnerability is a weakness in software, configuration or process that an attacker could exploit. Examples are an unpatched library, a default password or an open storage bucket. Vulnerabilities are found by scanning, testing and reports, then fixed by priority.

Vulnerability scanning uses automated tools to check systems, containers or code dependencies for known vulnerabilities. It runs regularly and in CI. Results are triaged so the most serious and reachable issues get fixed first.

A CVE, common vulnerabilities and exposures entry, is a public ID for a specific known vulnerability, like CVE followed by a year and number. It lets everyone refer to the same flaw. Scanners report findings by CVE ID.

CVSS, common vulnerability scoring system, gives a vulnerability a score from 0 to 10 based on how easy it is to exploit and how bad the impact is. Teams use it to prioritize fixes. Your own context, like whether the system is exposed, also matters.

Patching is applying vendor updates that fix bugs and security flaws. Patch management decides what to patch, tests it and rolls it out on a schedule. In regulated environments, patches to validated systems go through change control.

An SBOM, software bill of materials, is a list of all the components and libraries inside a piece of software, with versions. It lets you quickly check if you are affected by a new vulnerability. Regulators, including the FDA for connected medical devices, expect one.

Penetration testing is an authorized simulated attack on a system to find exploitable weaknesses. Skilled testers try to get in the way a real attacker would and report what they found. It is often required before go-live and periodically after.

A bug bounty program pays outside researchers for responsibly reporting security flaws. A vulnerability disclosure policy tells people how to report issues safely. Both bring more eyes onto a product's security.

An identity provider, IdP, is the system that stores user identities and handles login for other applications, such as Microsoft Entra ID or Okta. Apps trust the IdP instead of keeping their own passwords. It is the base for SSO and central access control.

OpenID Connect, OIDC, is a login standard built on OAuth 2.0. OAuth handles permission to access resources, and OIDC adds a standard way to prove who the user is, with an ID token. It is the common way modern apps do single sign-on.

SAML, security assertion markup language, is an older XML-based standard for single sign-on. The identity provider sends the app a signed assertion saying who the user is. Many enterprise apps still use SAML, while newer ones prefer OpenID Connect.

IAM, identity and access management, is how an organization manages who users and services are and what they can access. It covers accounts, roles, permissions, login and reviews. In the cloud, IAM policies control every action on every resource.

RBAC, role-based access control, gives permissions to roles, such as reviewer or approver, and assigns users to roles. It is simple to manage and audit. It struggles when access depends on details like site or product.

ABAC, attribute-based access control, decides access using attributes of the user, resource and context, such as department, site, data class and time. It is more flexible than RBAC. The rules are harder to understand and test.

Privileged access management, PAM, controls and monitors accounts with high power, like administrators and database owners. Typical controls are just-in-time access, approval, session recording and password vaulting. These accounts are the main target for attackers.

A passkey is a passwordless login using a key pair stored on your device, unlocked with a fingerprint, face or PIN. It is based on the FIDO2 and WebAuthn standards. Passkeys resist phishing because nothing reusable is typed or sent.
A password manager stores your passwords encrypted and fills them in for you. It makes unique strong passwords for every site practical. Protect it with a strong master password and MFA.

An encryption key is the secret value used to encrypt and decrypt data. Security depends on keeping keys secret, not on hiding the method. Keys should be stored in a key management service and rotated regularly.

A key management service, KMS, creates, stores and controls the use of encryption keys, with access logs. A hardware security module, HSM, is tamper-resistant hardware that keeps keys inside it. BYOK, bring your own key, lets a customer control the keys a cloud service uses.

A digital signature uses a private key to sign data so anyone with the matching public key can check who signed it and that it was not changed. It is used for software updates, documents and certificates. It is different from simply scanning a handwritten signature.

A digital certificate is an electronic document that binds a public key to an identity, such as a website domain, and is signed by a trusted certificate authority. Browsers check it to confirm they are talking to the real site. Certificates expire and must be renewed.

A certificate authority, CA, is a trusted organization that issues digital certificates after checking identity. Browsers and operating systems ship with a list of trusted root CAs. Companies also run private CAs for internal systems.

PKI, public key infrastructure, is the full system of certificate authorities, certificates, policies and tools used to issue, trust and revoke public keys. It underpins HTTPS, signed email, code signing and device identity. Large organizations run their own internal PKI.

entries.q: What is tokenization in data security?
entries.a: In data security, tokenization replaces a sensitive value, like a card number or patient ID, with a random token that has no meaning on its own. The real value stays in a protected vault. This is different from tokens in language models.
